summary: The smallest and most densely populated country in Central America, on the Pacific coast, known for its volcanic landscape and rebuilt after its civil war of the 1980s.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1524 the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Alvarado invaded El Salvador and conquered the Kingdom of Cuscatlán of the Pipil, and Catholicism arrived with colonial rule. In the colonial period Catholicism was the only legal religion, and the Church dominated education and social life. In the 1970s Archbishop Romero publicly criticized the military government's human rights abuses and was assassinated in 1980 while celebrating Mass, one of the triggers of the civil war; he was canonized by Pope Francis in 2018. Catholicism remains the largest religion, but its share has fallen sharply from more than ninety percent in the past.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical)
ranking.description: Protestantism was first introduced by American missionaries in 1896 but long remained a minority. During the civil war of 1980–1992, many people turned to evangelical and Pentecostal churches amid violence and displacement, since these churches offered mutual-aid networks and spiritual comfort and, unlike the Catholic Church, had not been drawn into the political conflict. After the war the evangelicals continued to grow rapidly, large churches arose in San Salvador, and their share rose to more than thirty percent.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has increased markedly since the 1990s, mainly among young people in cities. The politicization of religion during the civil war, church scandals, and urbanization and the spread of the internet have all alienated some young people from religious institutions. However, many who identify as non-religious still believe in God and simply do not belong to any church.

ranking.name: Others
ranking.description: Other religions include Jehovah's Witnesses, Mormons, and small numbers of Jews, Muslims and followers of indigenous traditional beliefs. From the late 19th century there have also been Arab Christian immigrants from Palestine, who have had influence in commerce and politics.

religion.background: The indigenous Pipil of El Salvador followed a polytheistic religion similar to that of the Aztecs. After the Spanish conquest in 1524 Catholicism became the state religion. After independence in the 19th century liberal governments restricted the Church's power. During the civil war of the 1980s, Archbishop Romero was assassinated, and liberation theology clashed fiercely with the military government. After the war the evangelicals grew rapidly, and El Salvador changed from a Catholic country into a society in which Catholics and evangelicals coexist.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish became the language of administration, religion and education of the colony after the Spanish conquest in 1524. The Pipil language (a branch of Nahuatl), which had been in common use, gradually withered during the colonial period; in the 'Matanza' (La Matanza) of 1932, when the military government suppressed a peasant uprising, thousands of indigenous people were killed, and survivors gave up indigenous languages and dress to avoid persecution, accelerating the complete spread of Spanish. Today almost the whole country speaks Spanish as its mother tongue.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English is mainly used by Salvadorans who have worked or lived in the United States and returned. During the civil war of the 1980s large numbers of Salvadorans emigrated to the United States, and today the diaspora numbers more than two million; close ties with the United States have made English increasingly common among young people and in business, and in 2001 El Salvador even adopted the US dollar as legal tender.

language.history: Before the Spanish conquest, indigenous languages such as Pipil and Lenca were in common use in El Salvador. After the Spanish conquest of 1524 Spanish became the mainstream language, and the indigenous languages gradually withered. After the 1932 massacre the indigenous languages were severely suppressed, Pipil came close to extinction, and today only a very few elderly people can use it. In recent years the government and academic institutions have promoted Pipil revitalization programs, with the language taught in some schools.

ranking.name: Pupusa
ranking.description: Corn dough is filled with cheese, chicharrón (ground pork) or refried beans, pressed into a thick round cake and griddled on a pan, served with curtido (pickled cabbage) and tomato sauce.
ranking.history: Pupusas originated with the pre-Columbian Pipil, and archaeologists have found implements for making corn foods at the Joya de Cerén site (a village buried by volcanic ash around AD 600, called the 'Pompeii of the Americas'). From the 1960s pupusas spread from the countryside to the cities, and during the civil war they spread to the United States with emigrants. In 2005 the Salvadoran legislature designated it the national dish, and the second Sunday of November each year is 'National Pupusa Day'.

ranking.name: Curtido (pickled cabbage slaw)
ranking.description: Cabbage, carrots and onions are shredded and pickled for several days with vinegar, oregano and chili, with a slight fermented tang and a crisp texture.
ranking.history: Curtido is made in a way similar to German sauerkraut and is generally thought to be related to the vinegar-pickling techniques brought by the Spanish, and cabbage and carrots were also crops introduced only in the colonial period. It is an indispensable side dish for pupusas, used to balance their greasiness. In El Salvador, every pupusa stall has its own curtido recipe, often kept in large glass jars for customers to help themselves.

ranking.name: Tamales
ranking.description: Corn dough is filled with chicken, pork, potatoes and sauce, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed for several hours, with a soft, moist texture.
ranking.history: Corn tamales have been a traditional food of the indigenous peoples of Central America for thousands of years, and the Maya and Aztecs used them as offerings in religious rites. After the Spanish arrived, new fillings such as chicken and pork were added. In El Salvador tamales are an essential food at Christmas and New Year, and households make them together before the holidays and distribute them to relatives and friends.

ranking.name: Horchata de morro
ranking.description: Morro seeds (the seeds of a gourd tree), rice, cacao, cinnamon, sesame and peanuts are ground into a powder and mixed with water or milk and sugar into an ice-cold drink, with a rich, fragrant flavor.
ranking.history: 'Horchata' originated in the drink made from tiger nuts in Valencia, Spain, and after Spanish colonists took it to the Americas, different places adopted local ingredients. The Salvadoran version uses morro seeds and cacao, which the indigenous people have long eaten, and cacao was even used as currency in the pre-Columbian period. It is one of El Salvador's most popular drinks and is often drunk with pupusas.

ranking.name: Atol de elote (sweet corn hot drink)
ranking.description: Fresh young corn kernels are ground and simmered with milk, sugar and cinnamon into a thick hot drink, with a sweet, creamy texture, often sprinkled with cinnamon powder and drunk hot.
ranking.history: 'Atol' comes from the Nahuatl 'atolli' and is a traditional drink the indigenous peoples of Central America have made from corn for thousands of years. In El Salvador, atol de elote is most common in the corn harvest season from August to September and has traditionally been associated with celebrations of the corn harvest. It is also often drunk on cold mornings or in the evening, with sweet bread or tamales.
